meta.titre: Digestive Secretions: which juice does what, and where
meta.sous_theme: Saliva, gastric juice, bile, pancreatic juice and intestinal juice

source.epreuve_titre: GCE O/L Human Biology past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: After a plate of fufu and njama njama at lunch in Douala, you do not feel the food being broken down, yet your body is hard at work. Glands in the mouth, the stomach wall, the liver, the pancreas and the small intestine pour out juices that turn large food molecules into small ones that the blood can carry. GCE questions ask you to name the juice, the enzyme, the place and the product, and one wrong link in the chain costs the mark. This course gives you the chain, gland by gland.

items: Digestion is the breakdown of large insoluble food molecules into small soluble molecules that can be absorbed.
Enzymes are protein catalysts; each one acts on one kind of substance and works best at a particular pH and temperature.
The alimentary canal runs from the mouth through the oesophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine to the anus.

sections.titre: Five digestive secretions: source, site of action and effect
sections.contenu_markdown:
### The chain of secretions

Each digestive juice is made by a gland, poured into the gut at a particular place, and contains substances suited to the food found there.

| Secretion | Made by | Acts in | Contents and action |
|---|---|---|---|
| Saliva | Salivary glands | Mouth | Salivary amylase changes starch to maltose; mucus lubricates the food |
| Gastric juice | Glands in the stomach wall | Stomach | Hydrochloric acid kills many microbes and gives an acid medium; pepsin changes proteins to shorter peptides; mucus coats the stomach lining |
| Bile | Liver (stored in the gall bladder) | Duodenum | No enzymes; bile salts emulsify fats; it is alkaline and neutralises the acid food from the stomach |
| Pancreatic juice | Pancreas | Duodenum | Amylase (starch to maltose), trypsin (proteins to peptides), lipase (fats to fatty acids and glycerol); alkaline |
| Intestinal juice | Glands in the wall of the small intestine | Ileum | Maltase (maltose to glucose), sucrase, lactase, and peptidases (peptides to amino acids) |

### Points that examiners test

- **Starch is digested in two stages.** Amylase gives maltose, then maltase gives glucose. Amylase never produces glucose directly.
- **The stomach wall is protected.** Pepsin is released in an inactive form that the acid activates, and a layer of mucus separates the acid and the enzyme from the cells of the wall.
- **Bile is not an enzyme.** Emulsification is a physical change: large fat droplets are broken into tiny droplets, which gives a bigger surface area for lipase to act on. No chemical change occurs.
- **pH matters.** Pepsin works best in acid (about pH 2), amylase near neutral, and the pancreatic and intestinal enzymes in slightly alkaline conditions. This is why bile and pancreatic juice neutralise the acid food that leaves the stomach.
- **End products.** Carbohydrates give glucose, proteins give amino acids, and fats give fatty acids and glycerol.

variantes.nom: Name the enzyme, the substrate or the product
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question gives one item of a pair and asks for the other.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
Memorise each enzyme as a triple:

| Enzyme | Substrate | Product |
|---|---|---|
| Salivary or pancreatic amylase | Starch | Maltose |
| Pepsin or trypsin | Protein | Peptides |
| Peptidases | Peptides | Amino acids |
| Lipase | Fats | Fatty acids and glycerol |
| Maltase | Maltose | Glucose |

variantes.nom: Describe the role of an organ
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question names the liver, the pancreas or a gland and gives several marks.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Use three moves: say **what the organ makes**, say **where it goes** (through a duct into the duodenum), and say **what the secretion does** there. For the liver: it makes bile, which is stored in the gall bladder and carried by the bile duct to the duodenum, where it emulsifies fats and neutralises acid. For the pancreas: it makes pancreatic juice, carried by the pancreatic duct to the duodenum, where its enzymes digest starch, proteins and fats.

sections.enonce_markdown: A girl eats a lunch of boiled rice with a beans stew. Describe how the starch and the protein in the meal are chemically digested between the mouth and the end of the small intestine. *(7 marks)*

etapes.action: Read the command word and list the nutrients.
etapes.justification: "Describe" asks for what happens, region by region. Rice supplies starch and beans supply protein, so two digestion chains are needed.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Plan: mouth, stomach, duodenum, ileum, with starch and protein in each.

etapes.justification: Saliva is the first secretion the food meets and it contains an enzyme for starch only.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Salivary amylase changes some starch to maltose. Protein is not digested in the mouth.

etapes.justification: The stomach gives acid conditions, which stop salivary amylase but allow the protein enzyme to work.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Pepsin, with hydrochloric acid, changes proteins to shorter peptides.

etapes.justification: The acid food must be neutralised before pancreatic enzymes can work well, and the pancreas supplies both a neutralising juice and enzymes.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Bile and pancreatic juice neutralise the acid. Pancreatic amylase changes the remaining starch to maltose; trypsin changes proteins to peptides.

etapes.action: Deal with the ileum and give the end products.
etapes.justification: The last step changes the intermediate products into the small molecules that can be absorbed.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Maltase changes maltose to glucose; peptidases change peptides to amino acids.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **Model answer.** In the mouth, salivary amylase digests some starch to maltose. In the stomach, hydrochloric acid and pepsin digest protein to peptides. In the duodenum, bile and pancreatic juice neutralise the acid; pancreatic amylase changes starch to maltose and trypsin changes protein to peptides. In the ileum, maltase changes maltose to glucose and peptidases change peptides to amino acids. The end products are glucose and amino acids.

items.erreur_markdown: "Bile contains an enzyme that digests fats."
items.pourquoi_faux: Bile contains no enzymes. Its bile salts only emulsify fat; the enzyme that digests fat is lipase, made by the pancreas.
items.correction_markdown: Bile **emulsifies** fat (physical change) and lipase **digests** it (chemical change) into fatty acids and glycerol.

items.erreur_markdown: "Pancreatic amylase breaks starch down into glucose."
items.pourquoi_faux: Amylase acts on starch to give the double sugar maltose. A second enzyme, maltase, is needed to change maltose to glucose.
items.correction_markdown: Write: starch, then maltose (amylase), then glucose (maltase, in the small intestine).

items.erreur_markdown: "Hydrochloric acid digests the protein in the stomach."
items.pourquoi_faux: Acid is not an enzyme. It kills microbes, activates pepsin and gives the acid medium in which pepsin works; the enzyme digests the protein.
items.correction_markdown: Pepsin digests protein to peptides; hydrochloric acid supplies the right pH.

items.erreur_markdown: "Bile is made in the gall bladder."
items.pourquoi_faux: The gall bladder only stores and releases bile; the liver makes it.
items.correction_markdown: The liver makes bile, the gall bladder stores it, and the bile duct carries it to the duodenum.

items.enonce_markdown: Name: (a) the organ that makes bile; (b) the organ that stores bile; (c) the enzyme found in saliva; (d) the sugar produced when maltase acts on maltose; (e) the enzyme that digests fats.

A student set up four test tubes, each with 5 cm³ of starch solution. Tube 1 received 1 cm³ of fresh saliva and was kept at 37 °C. Tube 2 received 1 cm³ of boiled saliva at 37 °C. Tube 3 received 1 cm³ of fresh saliva and was kept in ice-cold water. Tube 4 received 1 cm³ of distilled water at 37 °C. After 20 minutes a sample from each tube was tested with iodine solution, and another sample was tested with Benedict's solution (heated). Predict the results and explain tubes 1, 2 and 3.
items.solution_markdown: Tube 1: iodine stays yellow-brown (no starch left); Benedict's gives an orange or brick-red precipitate, because salivary amylase has changed starch to maltose, a reducing sugar. Tube 2: iodine turns blue-black and Benedict's stays blue, because boiling has **denatured** the enzyme. Tube 3: mostly blue-black with iodine and little or no colour change with Benedict's, because at low temperature the enzyme is **inactive or very slow**, not destroyed; it would work again if warmed. Tube 4 is the control: blue-black with iodine and blue with Benedict's, showing that the water alone does not digest starch.

items.enonce_markdown: A patient has a stone that blocks the bile duct. (a) Explain two effects of this on the digestion of a fatty meal. (b) Suggest why the faeces become pale. (c) Explain why the digestion of starch and protein carries on almost normally.
items.solution_markdown: (a) Bile cannot reach the duodenum, so fats are **not emulsified**: the droplets stay large, the surface area for lipase is small, and fat digestion is slow, so some fat passes out undigested. Also, the acid food is less well neutralised, so enzymes in the duodenum work less well, and the fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K) are poorly absorbed. (b) Bile pigments, which give faeces their brown colour, no longer reach the gut. (c) Amylase, trypsin, maltase and peptidases do not need bile to act, and pancreatic juice still enters the duodenum. **Fat digestion is the one most affected.**

items_markdown: Saliva (salivary glands), gastric juice (stomach wall), bile (liver), pancreatic juice (pancreas) and intestinal juice (small intestine wall) are the five secretions.
Amylase changes starch to maltose; maltase changes maltose to glucose; pepsin and trypsin change proteins to peptides; peptidases give amino acids; lipase gives fatty acids and glycerol.
Bile has no enzymes: it emulsifies fats and neutralises the acid food from the stomach.
Hydrochloric acid supplies the pH for pepsin and kills microbes; mucus protects the stomach wall.
In a role question, say what the organ makes, where it goes and what it does there.
